Same for backticks/`$()` anywhere in the command. The old grep-based check would have caught this; the new one does not.
findings.suggestion: strip `$(` / `` ` `` / `${` sequences before tokenizing (or treat them as segment separators, like `;`), so nested commands are parsed rather than silently dropped.  2. Category: bug — Inline trailing comments are parsed as push arguments (false positive)

findings.file: force_push_guard.py` — `_tokens()` sets `lex.commenters = ""` with the comment "bash treats # as a comment only at word start", but the word-start rule is never implemented
findings.finding: git push -f origin feature/x # pushing fix for main` tokenizes `#`, `pushing`, ... `main` as push arguments; `main` becomes a "refspec" with `forced=True`, so a legitimate force push to a feature branch is blocked. findings.suggestion: drop tokens from a word-start `#` to end of line (a `#` token or a token beginning with `#` after whitespace terminates the segment as bash does), rather than disabling comment handling altogether.  3. Category: bug — `_exe_index` mishandles wrappers with non-option arguments

findings.finding: timeout 10 git push -f origin main` — `timeout` is a WRAPPER, but `10` doesn't start with `-`, so the loop returns the index of `10` as the executable. The push is never inspected. Tests only cover `sudo -u bob git` (option+value) and bare wrappers; `timeout <duration>` — a very common wrapper — silently bypasses the guard.
findings.suggestion: for value-taking wrappers with non-clustered value arguments, skip the wrapper's trailing non-option arguments too (or special-case `timeout`, which takes a mandatory duration operand), or scan forward for a `git` token when a wrapper's operand position doesn't resolve to an executable.  4. findings.finding: arg == "--force" or arg.startswith("--force-with-lease")` misses `--force-if-includes`, which (combined with `--force-with-lease` or a `+refspec`) forces the push. Low impact since it requires a `+`/lease flag too, which are matched, but `git push origin +main` is caught — so this is minor.
findings.suggestion: match any `--force` long option, or add `--force-if-includes` explicitly.  5. Category: test — tests mirror the implementation's blind spots

findings.finding: Coverage is broad and genuinely behavioral (exit codes asserted, both directions), but all wrapper tests use forms that happen to work (`sudo -u bob`, bare `xargs`/`env`/`time`); no case for `timeout 30 git push -f origin main`, `$(...)` substitution, or trailing comments. A wrong-but-tested implementation passes while the cases above slip through. The `_bash()` CI-hardening and fail-open tests are good.
findings.suggestion: add regression cases for `timeout 10 git push -f origin main`, `echo $(git push -f origin main)`, and `git push -f origin feature/x # fix main`.  Non-issues checked: the two spec false positives (branch name containing `-f`, `--notes-file` + unrelated `checkout master`) are fixed and covered; `--force-with-lease` is explicit per spec; fail-open error path is intentional and tested; the validate_command.sh plumbing (bytes I/O for cp1252, exit-code propagation) is correct and preserves the existing block contract (exit 2, same message).

findings.finding: Inline shell comments are parsed as push arguments. For example, `git push origin feature/x # --force main` is blocked even though Bash executes only a normal push to `feature/x`. This violates the requirement to inspect actual push arguments.
findings.suggestion: Recognize unquoted comments beginning at word boundaries while preserving literal mid-word `#` characters.

findings.finding: Splitting into lines before tokenization loses multiline quote boundaries. A harmless command such as `git commit -m "release notes\n git push -f origin main\n"` is blocked because its message content is interpreted as a separate command.
findings.suggestion: Preserve quote state across newlines and split commands only at unquoted separators. Add a regression test with a multiline quoted message containing force-push text.

findings.finding: Implicit push destinations are inferred from the hook’s repository and both HEAD/upstream names, rather than the command’s actual destination. `cd repo && git push -f` can therefore pass when `repo` is on `main` but the hook’s repository is on a feature branch. Conversely, with `push.default=current`, a feature branch tracking `origin/main` is incorrectly blocked even though it pushes to the feature branch.
findings.suggestion: Track the effective working directory and resolve implicit destinations using the selected remote and Git push configuration. Cover both directory changes and differing `push.default` behavior with repository-backed tests.  The two reported false positives have regression coverage, but the replacement introduces additional false blocks and can miss protected-branch pushes. Ship-with-fixes.  SHIPWRIGHT_VERDICT: revise
